title: Word Dictionary With Wildcards
statement:
Build a dictionary of lowercase words that can be searched with a simple pattern.

  • WordDictionary() creates an empty dictionary.
  • addWord(word) adds word.
  • search(pattern) returns true if some added word matches pattern. A letter matches only itself. A dot . matches exactly one letter, any letter. The match covers the whole word: the pattern and the word have the same length.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the dictionary. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.out: [null, null, null, true, true, true, false]
examples.why: Each dot stands for one letter, so "l.mp" fits both words. "lam" is only the start of "lamp", and a search must match a whole word.
A dot is never zero or two letters. Only patterns of length 3 can match "sun".

examples.out: [null, null, null, null, true, true, false]
examples.why: For "b.g" the dot first tries "a", which leads nowhere, and must then try "e". Following only one branch at a dot misses the answer.

constraints: Added words use lowercase English letters
Patterns use lowercase letters and at most 2 dots
hints: Without dots this is the plain prefix-tree lookup. What changes at a dot?
At a dot you do not know which child to take, so try every child. That is a depth-first search that can back out of a branch.
Write match(node, i): if i is the pattern's length, return whether a word ends at node. On a letter, follow that one child. On a dot, return true if match(child, i + 1) is true for any child.

explain.intuition:
Store the words in a trie, exactly as for plain prefix search. A pattern without dots is then a straight walk from the root. A dot means "any one letter", so at that position the walk has to split and try every child. If one branch fails further down, you back up and try the next. That is depth-first search over the trie, guided by the pattern.

The trie is what keeps this cheap. A dot only branches into letters that actually continue some stored word, and a fixed letter cuts all other branches at once. Compare that with checking the pattern against every stored word, which costs the whole dictionary on every search.
steps: Build a trie: each node has kids (letter → node) and end (a word stops here). addWord is the usual insert.
If pattern[i] is a letter, follow that child, or return false if it is missing.
If it is a dot, loop over every child and return true as soon as match(child, i + 1) is true. Return false after the loop.
pitfalls: Returning true when the pattern runs out instead of node.end. Then "rea." matches because "react" passes through, though no 4-letter word was added.
At a dot, returning the result of the first child only. On example 3, "b.g" tries "ba", fails, and wrongly gives up.
Treating a dot as "any number of letters", like * in a glob. Here it is exactly one letter, so lengths must match.

complexity.time: O(L) to add; O(L) to search without dots, up to O(26² · L) with two dots

solutions.title: Compare the pattern with every word
solutions.idea: Keep a plain list of words. For a search, check every word of the same length letter by letter, letting a dot match anything.

solutions.title: Trie + depth-first search at dots
solutions.idea: Walk the trie along the pattern. A letter follows one child; a dot tries every child and backs out of branches that fail.
solutions.time: O(L) add, O(26^d · L) search with d dots

followups: Patterns may now hold any number of dots. What is the worst case, and would grouping words by length help?
Add a * that matches zero or more letters. How does the search change?
